title: Illustrative Tax Scenario Evidence Lab
contexts: S corporation readiness
An illustrative business owner is considering a change in tax classification while the operating model is changing.
ownership records; current profit; payroll readiness; owner duties; state questions
The business has stable sales but the owner has not documented duties or recurring administration costs.
A modeled advantage is a starting question, not evidence that the election is appropriate.
Owner reimbursement review
An illustrative owner has personally paid costs described as business-related and wants a review of the reporting process.
expense receipts; business purpose; reimbursement policy; payment history; entity records
The ledger contains transfers labeled reimbursements without attached expense support.
Review the records and procedure before assigning tax treatment to the transfers.
Estimated tax update
An illustrative owner is updating a projection after income or withholding changed.
current books; payment proof; withholding; income forecast; prior projection
A large receipt changes the annual outlook after earlier payments were calculated.
Distinguish updated assumptions from a verified payment record.
Retirement funding decision
An illustrative business is considering a retirement plan while employment and compensation are changing.
employee census; wages; provider quotes; plan documents; funding calendar
The owner's desired contribution is modeled without a current employee census.
The contribution model cannot substitute for plan design and implementation review.
STR depreciation decision
An illustrative short-term rental owner is evaluating a study alongside activity and household facts.
guest stays; task records; property basis; depreciation history; study quote
The study estimate is available but the activity records are incomplete.
Keep the depreciation estimate separate from the question of current loss usability.
Long-term rental study decision
An illustrative landlord wants to compare a study with continuing the existing depreciation schedule.
acquisition records; improvement history; suspended amounts; holding period; preparer scope
The property has a large projected deduction but the owner's current income picture is missing.
The decision depends on timing, limitations and total implementation cost.
C corporation retention decision
An illustrative business owner is considering retained earnings and future personal cash needs.
operating forecast; compensation; distribution plans; capital needs; entity costs
A model compares current entity rates without a plan for later owner withdrawals.
Compare the full cash path and future assumptions with professional guidance.
Entity loan reconciliation
An illustrative owner has advanced funds to an entity and later receives payments.
agreements; bank transfers; ledger balances; repayment terms; ownership records
The ledger labels all owner transfers as loans even though the documents differ.
Reconcile the transaction history and ask the preparer to determine the treatment.
Business sale preparation
An illustrative owner is reviewing draft sale terms and the available records.
draft agreement; asset history; ownership; allocation proposal; closing costs
The proposed headline price changes while the form of the transaction remains unsettled.
The after-tax comparison requires the actual structure and source records.
Prior-year correction review
An illustrative taxpayer discovers a possible issue in returns prepared in earlier years.
filed returns; workpapers; source records; correspondence; year-by-year issue list
A new advisor sees a missing schedule but has not established what was previously reported.
Reconstruct the history before selecting a correction procedure.
tasks: Missing ownership evidence
Test the conclusion against an unresolved owner or reporting entity.

List the assumed owner, actual title records and agreement evidence. Mark the tax-reporting question for professional review rather than filling the gap with the most favorable taxpayer. Rebuild the comparison if the responsible entity changes.
A revised assumption list and ownership question.
The illustration silently treats legal title and tax reporting as the same.
What ownership facts must be resolved before the illustration can be applied?
assumed owner; title source; reporting entity; agreement; open ownership question
Incomplete financial records
Distinguish a model input from verified books.

Identify the statements used, cutoff date and unresolved balances. Explain whether missing information could change the baseline or proposed result. An illustration's precision does not make an incomplete input reliable.
A supported baseline with uncertainty marked.
The example uses a precise number from provisional records.
Which balances or periods need reconciliation before modeling alternatives?
statement source; cutoff date; unresolved balance; baseline effect; verification owner
Date ambiguity
Expose the different dates the illustration depends on.

Separate agreement, payment, transfer, completion and filing dates as relevant. Ask the professional which date controls each decision. Do not use a convenient date simply because the other records are missing.
A dated assumption map.
One date is used for several events with different evidence.
Which date facts change the applicable review and what supports them?
assumed date; event; source record; alternative date; review question
Unverified payment
Test whether the example confuses an obligation with an actual payment.

Trace the amount, recipient, date and bank or provider evidence. Separate a planned payment from completed transfer or reported treatment. Update the illustration only after documenting what actually happened.
A payment-to-reporting bridge.
A planned payment is treated as settled evidence.
What was paid, to whom, when and how was it reported?
obligation; actual payment; recipient; payment proof; reporting status
Missing expense detail
Identify the cost pool the example actually analyzes.

Separate purpose, payer, invoice support and cost adjustments. Ask which amounts require tax classification rather than assuming every cash outlay has the same treatment. Record missing or overlapping cost records.
A source-supported cost pool.
A single total combines unrelated spending or duplicate entries.
Which source amounts and treatment questions must be separated?
cost description; payer; invoice; adjustment; unresolved treatment
Third-party role gap
Review what other people actually do in the fact pattern.

List operational, professional and implementation roles with the evidence supporting each. Do not assume an owner performed all work or that a provider completed every step. Identify which role matters to the question being modeled.
A role and evidence map.
The example leaves material helper or professional work unstated.
Whose work or decision responsibility changes the fact pattern?
person role; task; record source; owner involvement; review significance
Unknown prior reporting
Test the example against the treatment already reported.

Gather earlier returns and workpapers, then compare the model with the known history. Mark missing schedules clearly. A favorable correction is not established merely because an owner lacks a copy of an earlier record.
A prior-versus-proposed treatment register.
The model assumes an earlier position without reading the return.
What was already reported and what history must be reconstructed?
tax year; filed treatment; workpaper; proposed change; history gap
No baseline alternative
Build the comparison the headline leaves out.

Describe what happens without the proposed action, including costs and timing. Compare the same facts and period for both options. A proposed deduction does not by itself identify incremental financial benefit.
A like-for-like alternative comparison.
The headline compares a full proposed benefit with no baseline.
What is the supported alternative and which assumptions differ?
baseline action; proposed action; common period; changed input; comparison question
Undefined implementation scope
Identify the steps required after the recommendation.

List the document, decision maker, implementation professional and follow-up evidence for each step. Distinguish educational modeling from purchased implementation. Ask which tasks need a separate scope before treating the plan as achievable.
An implementation dependency register.
The illustration assumes work outside the engagement will be completed.
Who performs each action and what conditions must be satisfied first?
recommendation; prerequisite; action owner; scope boundary; completion evidence
Fees omitted
Add the costs necessary to execute and maintain the proposal.

Separate initial fees, recurring administration and third-party work. Use a clearly stated period for comparing options. Do not treat implementation expense as zero because the illustration focuses on one tax concept.
A cost-adjusted comparison file.
A gross modeled benefit is presented as net value.
Which initial and recurring costs affect the proposed comparison?
initial expense; recurring expense; third-party fee; comparison period; missing quote
State treatment untested
Keep federal and state questions visible as separate inputs.

List relevant jurisdictions and the assumptions used in the model. Ask the preparer to review conformity, entity obligations or other jurisdiction-specific issues. Do not automatically apply a federal outcome to every state.
A jurisdiction assumption register.
The federal result is reused as the combined tax result.
Which state facts and calculations need independent review?
jurisdiction; federal input; state assumption; filing responsibility; review question
Future transaction ignored
Extend the illustration to a possible sale, exit or later owner cash need.

Record the future event and the assumptions the initial model omits. Ask for a complete timing and cash comparison. Do not convert a first-year timing effect into a permanent benefit without addressing later consequences.
An initial-and-future decision map.
The headline stops before a material future event.
How does the expected future transaction change the comparison?
future event; expected timing; omitted assumption; cash need; follow-up review
masters: Baseline alternative builder
Build the missing comparison beside an illustrative planning proposal.
baseline; proposed action; common assumptions; changed facts; unresolved input
Deduction versus tax-change worksheet
Separate a stated deduction from a modeled tax effect and implementation costs.
deduction; assumed rate; gross model; costs; limitations
Timing benefit review map
Keep initial and later effects separate in an illustrative comparison.
initial effect; later event; holding period; future assumption; review question
Scenario evidence gate register
Record which assumptions are supported and which need review.
assumption; source; evidence status; consequence; reviewer
Proposed implemented verified tracker
Keep planning stages distinct rather than treating a delivered model as a realized result.
recommendation; approval; implementation; reported treatment; verification
Sensitivity question builder
Ask how a changed assumption would alter an illustrative comparison.
input; baseline value; alternative; affected decision; review question
Scenario to consultation brief
Convert an illustrative example into an individualized review question.
decision; actual facts; records; deadline; engagement question
